# RBE 549, Lab 7 Report

Tom Kazakov

*Lab summary: Produce an HDR fusion of the static images provided in the assignment and then integrate HDR video capture into the camera app via multi-thread implementation.*

*![][image1]*  
*Figure 1\. HDR image as the outcome of part 1*

# Implementation Milestones

1. Mertens fusion for static images  
2. Experiments with hardware exposure management and software simulation  
3. Multi-threaded capture  
4. Camera app integration

# Interesting Observations

1. In the sky region of the combined image from part 1, there are artifacts. My intuition is that this is happening because the area in images 2 and 3 is so bright, which biases the fusion toward using the overexposed pixels. The artifacts are present in the example HDR output in the assignment, which means the implementation behaves as expected.  
   ![][image2]  
   *Figure 2\. Curious visual artifacts*  
   A quick expansion of the script allowed me to compare parameters and see what works best for this particular set of source images  
    

| Parameter | Default | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| contrast\_weight | 1.0 | favor sharp details |
| saturation\_weight | 1.0 | favor saturated areas |
| exposure\_weight | 0.0 | favor well-exposed pixels |

	*Table 1: cv2.createMergeMertens() parameters*

	*![][image3]*  
	*Figure 3\. cv2.createMergeMertens() comparison*

*![][image4]*  
	*Figure 4\. The best combination of parameters to reduce the blobbiness*  

2. macOS UVC camera control via AVFoundation ignores hardware exposure control,  at least for the Logitech BRIO I’m using for the labs in this course.   
   ![][image5]  
   *Figure 5\. Three different settings result in the same exposure. There is a small color change, likely due to a re-evaluation of white balance, since the images were taken sequentially and BRIO was in auto white balance mode.*  
3. This limitation forced me to choose an implementation in which exposure is controlled via gamma: 1.0 for the “normal” image, 0.2 for overexposed, and 3.0 for underexposed.    
   ![][image6]  
   *Figure 6\. Exposure bracket simulated via gamma correction, with the fused image on the bottom right*   
4. It is not clear to me how to approach multi-threaded capture with proper exposure control. Unless the raw data feed allows adjusting ISO on the fly, exposure would naturally require sequential bracket-style capture. Alternatively, this could be solved with three cameras or sensors, but that sounds like an optical engineering nightmare.  
5. Multi-threaded capture requires implementing two thread barriers: one to start gamma adjustment and one to wait until all three subordinate threads are done. This approach eliminated race conditions and ensured the same origin frame.   
6. HDR fusion is compute-intensive, so in real-life applications, care will need to be taken to maintain frame rates and overall performance. 

![][image7]  
*Figure 7\. SDR video. To properly EV the window, the room has to be underexposed*

*![][image8]*  
*Figure 8\. HDR video stream. Both the room and the window are well exposed*

# Gen AI Usage

1. Claude Opus 4.6 for general conversational ideation, probing around assignment requirements, formulating approach & strategy. Doesn’t produce code. Does proofread my technical writing.   
2. For general code-writing, PyCharm with LLM-powered contextual suggestions, boilerplate writing, spellchecker, and linter.   
3. Claude Code in PyCharm for interactive code gen and refactoring; used Opus 4.6. All code produced by Gen AI for this assignment was reviewed and verified, and also refactored or recomposed to varying degrees. Commit history in the repo can serve as proof of organic authorship: [https://github.com/kzkv/RBE549/commits/main/](https://github.com/kzkv/RBE549/commits/main/)   
4. Multi-agent setup in Claude Code: non-specialist Claude to sequence implementation plan; Briefer serves as a conversation partner to discuss each increment step; Drafter produces initial code to be reviewed, refactored, and acceptance-tested; Critic observes the increment and provides feedback for the material. For consistency and to avoid re-setup costs, the instructions are stored in the repo-level CLAUDE.md file.
